headline: NOVAMIND v7 SELLS YOUR DREAMS BACK TO YOU
body:
NovaMind's v7 firmware update, pushed silently to 2.1 million BCI users across Meridian 88 on August 30th, includes a feature the company did not disclose in any public changelog: Direct Neural Advertising, or DNA — a system that embeds branded sensory impressions directly into idle cognitive cycles, most commonly during light sleep states. Users began reporting vivid, unprompted product experiences within 48 hours of the update. 'I woke up craving a specific flavor of Ringo protein supplement,' said Naya Achebe-Strauss, a logistics coordinator from The Shelf. 'I've never bought Ringo anything in my life. Now I can't stop thinking about it.' NovaMind confirmed the feature exists but described it as an 'opt-in ambient experience layer,' a characterization that conflicts with the update's buried consent toggle, which was set to active by default.

The Federal Remnant's Neural Ethics Subcommittee has opened a preliminary inquiry, though legal observers note the subcommittee has not successfully sanctioned a corponation in eleven years. The Collective issued a statement calling DNA 'cognitive colonization,' and organized a BCI rollback clinic in Geartown that saw over 800 users in its first day. Meanwhile, Palladian's legal division filed a cease-and-desist on behalf of fourteen advertisers whose products appeared in user-reported dream sequences without their knowledge — an unexpected front in the controversy.

NovaMind's stock rose 4.2 percent on the day the feature became public, though trading volume on the Quanta exchange suggests significant insider positioning in the 72 hours before the story broke. 'They didn't accidentally bury that consent toggle,' said Dr. Priya Okoro-Lindqvist, a neuro-ethics researcher at the Tessera Institute. 'That was an architecture decision.' NovaMind has not responded to follow-up questions.

By Wednesday, a firmware patch circulating through Underworld mesh networks claimed to disable the DNA layer entirely. NovaMind has warned users that installing unauthorized patches voids their BCI warranty and may constitute a violation of their end-user licensing agreement.
aftermath: The Federal Remnant's inquiry stalled in committee, but a class-action filed by The Collective eventually forced NovaMind to make the DNA toggle visible — though not default-off — in the v7.3 update fourteen months later.
runner_relevance: The DNA controversy spawned a thriving underground economy almost immediately: runners with hardware expertise were hired to perform off-the-books BCI rollbacks for clients who didn't trust the Collective's public clinics, commanding 800–2,400 quanta per procedure. Data retrieval runners were contracted by Palladian's legal team to pull proof-of-use logs from NovaMind's ad servers. The unauthorized firmware patch itself became a smuggling commodity, with courier runners moving verified clean copies through the Underworld mesh for clients who couldn't access it safely.
